analysis.one_liner: Expands Social Security benefits and funds them with new payroll taxes on income over $400,000.
analysis.headline: The Social Security 2100 Act, which would raise benefits for tens of millions of Americans and pay for it with new taxes on earnings and investment income above $400,000, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in July 2023 and received no hearing, vote, or further action before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make several permanent-feeling changes to Social Security for a ten-year period: an across-the-board benefit bump, a higher minimum benefit pegged to the poverty line for people who worked at low wages for decades, a more generous cost-of-living adjustment for seniors, caregiver credits for people who left work to care for family, an end to the five-month wait for disability benefits, repeal of two provisions that cut benefits for government retirees, and student benefits extended to age 26. It would pay for this by applying Social Security payroll taxes to all wages above $400,000 and by levying the Social Security tax on investment income of high earners.
analysis.who_benefits: Social Security beneficiaries, especially those at the bottom: long-term low earners get a minimum benefit tied to the federal poverty guideline; widows and widowers in two-income households get larger survivor benefits; people who spent years out of paid work caring for children or chronically dependent relatives earn Social Security credit; disabled workers no longer lose five months of benefits waiting; former state and local government workers stop having their benefits reduced; students whose parent died or retired can collect through age 26; and retirees get a cost-of-living formula better matched to senior spending. Disabled beneficiaries who work would see benefits reduced gradually instead of cut off, making returning to work less risky.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-wage retirees, disabled workers, caregivers, widows

how_it_helps.text: Raises the first benefit-formula factor from 90% to 93% of average earnings, an across-the-board increase payable 2025-2034 [S2][S3].
Sets a minimum benefit so that a worker with 30 or more years of work receives at least 125% of the poverty guideline, phasing up with years of work, payable 2025-2034 [S3].
Computes annual cost-of-living adjustments using whichever of the standard wage-earner index or the senior-specific CPI-E index produces the higher increase [S2][S3].

Repeals the windfall elimination provision and the government pension offset, which currently cut benefits for people who also earn a pension from work not covered by Social Security, such as many state and local government employees and teachers [S2][S3].

Eliminates the five-month waiting period for disability benefits and, instead of terminating disability benefits outright when a beneficiary earns above the limit, gradually reduces them $1 for each $2 earned over the threshold [S3].

Lets children of deceased, disabled, or retired workers keep collecting benefits through age 25 if they are at least half-time post-secondary students, and extends eligibility to children living with grandparents or other relatives [S2][S3].
Adds caregiver credits: up to five years of care for a young child or a chronically dependent relative count as deemed wages worth half the national average wage [S3].

Improves survivor benefits for widows and widowers in two-income households and increases benefits by 5% a year for beneficiaries 15 or more years past initial eligibility, phasing in over five years [S3].
Bars closing Social Security field offices, hearing offices, and rural contact stations unless conditions such as public hearings are met, and requires mailing account statements [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: High earners. Wages above $400,000 would become subject to the 12.4% Social Security payroll tax, split between employer and employee, with a special rule so workers with multiple employers only pay once; self-employed high earners pay the same through self-employment tax; and net investment income above the high-income threshold would bear a new 12.4% Social Security tax on top of the existing 3.8% Medicare tax. Earnings above $400,000 would also count a little in the benefit formula (1%), but most of the new revenue goes to other people's benefits. The bill also holds SSI, Medicaid, and CHIP beneficiaries harmless so the benefit increases do not cost them other aid.

drawbacks.text: The major benefit improvements are temporary: the across-the-board increase, higher minimum benefit, improved COLA, WEP/GPO repeal, and other boosts apply only for 2025-2034, after which primary insurance amounts must be recomputed back down [S3].

The financing falls on a narrow base: applying the full 12.4% payroll tax to wages above $400,000 and a 12.4% tax on high earners' net investment income is a large new tax on roughly the top slice of households, which critics would argue discourages work and investment at the top [S2][S3].

The new solvency revenue phases in slowly (an escalating add-on to the wage index from 0.5% to 0.9% after 2024) and the bill does not guarantee permanent solvency, so its trust-fund effect is limited to the decade it covers [S3].

Barring field-office closures without hearings and other conditions constrains the Social Security Administration's ability to reorganize its footprint as usage shifts, even when a closure might save money [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For most beneficiaries the gains are concrete and large: a bigger check, a poverty-level floor for career low earners, no waiting period for disability, and full benefits for government retirees. The main honest costs are that the improvements expire after 2034, so people would face benefit drops unless Congress extends them, and that the new taxes concentrate on households above $400,000 and on investment income. Whether those taxes are too heavy is a values question; the design choice to make benefits temporary while the politics of permanence stay unresolved is the bill's real weakness.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Finance Committee from July 2023 until the Congress ended, with no hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: Senator Richard Blumenthal introduced the Social Security 2100 Act on July 12, 2023, joined by Senators Whitehouse, Padilla, Duckworth, and Lujan [S1][S3][S4].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the day it was introduced [S5].
The action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action of any kind after the referral [S5].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 without the bill ever receiving a vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-income households that would have paid the new payroll and investment-income taxes are better off because the bill never advanced, as is anyone opposed to expanding Social Security's federal footprint; beneficiaries who would have received larger checks are worse off.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners who avoided the new taxes

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled four Democratic cosponsors

for.name: Sens. Whitehouse, Padilla, Duckworth, and Lujan
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors of the bill

against.name: Senate Finance Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill in the 18 months after referral

against.name: Senate majority leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor, which it could not reach without committee action

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so the party split on the merits is unknown; all five sponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored.

industries.industry: Households with wages or investment income above $400,000
industries.note: The bill removes the payroll tax cap above $400,000 and adds a 12.4% Social Security tax on high earners' net investment income; the money funds benefits for everyone else, so this group's cost is the public's gain.

industries.industry: State and local government pension systems and their retirees (teachers, public safety, municipal workers)
industries.note: Repealing the windfall elimination provision and government pension offset means these workers and their survivors would keep their full Social Security benefits alongside their government pensions, a long-sought fix that also ends an inequity for roughly 3 million public servants.
Self-employment income above $400,000 would be newly subject to the Social Security portion of the self-employment tax, with no employer to share the cost.

industries.industry: Social Security Administration (field offices and public services)
industries.note: The bill locks in the network of field offices, hearing offices, and rural contact stations by barring closures without hearings and other conditions, protecting in-person access for seniors and disabled applicants.
